## What

The text streaming path in `cli/src/utils/block-operations.ts` concatenated the whole accumulated block with each incoming delta and then ran two `String.includes` scans over the result:

```ts
const combinedText = lastBlock.content + text
if (combinedText.includes(THINK_OPEN_TAG) || combinedText.includes(THINK_CLOSE_TAG)) { ... }
```

That made one reply cost **O(n²) in its own length** — every delta re-walked everything before it, allocating and flattening the concatenation each time.

## Why it's safe to narrow the scan

A think tag can only be *completed* by the delta that completes it, at the seam between the block's tail and that delta. A tag already sitting inside the block was split out when it arrived. So the check now:

1. looks at the last 7 characters of the block (the widest partial tag, `</think`), plus the delta itself;
2. falls back to the original full-block scan whenever either contains `<`.

`<` in ordinary prose (`a < b`) still takes the full path, so nothing is lost.

## Measurement (`bun`, same machine, before → after)

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 8,000 deltas, 470 KB, plain text | 434 ms | **1.1 ms** |
| 4,000 deltas, 234 KB | 117 ms | **0.9 ms** |
| 2,000 deltas, 117 KB | 34 ms | **0.7 ms** |
| 1,000 deltas, 59 KB | 21 ms | **0.4 ms** |
| 8 subagents × 600 deltas | 38 ms | **5.5 ms** |

Cost is now linear in stream length instead of quadratic (`us/delta` was rising 17 → 54 as the stream grew; it now sits flat below 0.5).

Memory: no leak found on this path. The batched updater's interval is already disposed when a turn ends (`use-send-message.ts`), so it was not changed.

## Verification

- **Behavioural equivalence, not just tests:** 432 corpus scenarios (18 texts × 12 chunk sizes, root and agent paths) dumped from both implementations — **byte-identical** output, sha256 `6e06dde1…`.
- `bun test src/utils src/hooks` — **2672 pass, 0 fail** (157 files).
- `bun run typecheck` — exit 0.
- New `block-operations-streaming.test.ts` covers tags split inside the tag syntax at every seam position, the 7-char `</think` boundary, and long blocks keeping every character.

One pre-existing quirk surfaced while writing the tests and is left untouched: `<think></think>` with no content emits zero blocks, and a tag arriving after a long prefix folds the prefix into the reasoning block. Both behave identically before and after this change, hence the narrower assertions in the new test file.

ai.title: CLI stream text scans only the tag seam to avoid quadratic cost
ai.summary: The appendTextWithThinkParsingToBlocks function in cli/src/utils/block-operations.ts previously concatenated the entire accumulated block with each incoming delta, making think tag detection quadratic in stream length. It now computes a seam of at most seven characters (the widest partial tag minus one) and only runs the original full-block scan if that seam or the delta contains a less-than sign. Ordinary prose without angle brackets skips the allocation and scan entirely. Benchmarks in the PR show an 8,000-delta plain-text stream dropping from 434 ms to 1.1 ms.
ai.evidence: The diff in cli/src/utils/block-operations.ts replaces the unconditional full-string concatenation and includes scan in appendTextWithThinkParsingToBlocks with a seamLength calculation and a gate on seam.includes('<') that only triggers the full scan when a less-than character is present.

eli5.text: The tool now checks for special markers much faster as text arrives, by looking only at the very end of what it already has instead of re-reading the whole thing. This targets developers using the free coding assistant in their terminal or desktop app. Long responses no longer cause a noticeable slowdown in the app's processing, making it feel snappier when reading a large amount of text.

acceptedPr.title: perf(cli): render streaming markdown incrementally
acceptedPr.author: Salhi-zh
acceptedPr.body:
## Problem

`ContentWithMarkdown` re-renders the live message on every flush (~10/s) while it streams, and each render re-parsed the **entire accumulated answer** with unified + remark-gfm. `renderMarkdown` costs roughly **3 ms per kilobyte**, so:

| Answer size | Cost of one render |
|---|---|
| 10 KB | 35 ms |
| 50 KB | 115 ms |
| 200 KB | 480 ms |
| 500 KB | 1.4 s |

That is the stall users feel on long answers: the render thread blocks for hundreds of milliseconds per flush, and the total work for one stream is quadratic. `AgentMessage` did the same thing per subagent, so a fan-out of 8 agents paid 8 full parses per flush.

## Fix

Streaming text is append-only, so the parse of everything before the last complete block boundary is still valid on the next flush. `streaming-markdown.ts` keeps that prefix parsed and re-renders only the tail:

- boundaries are blank lines outside fenced code, and never next to a list or blockquote (a loose list or quote would be split, restarting ordered numbering);
- the trailing `\n\n` separator is held at the top level rather than inside the memoized segment, so the final trim behaves exactly like a single render;
- committed segments are wrapped in `memo`, so React stops re-walking the prefix at all - this is what took the worst flush from 38 ms to 3.8 ms;
- a width/palette change, or content that is not an extension of what was rendered (chat reload, edit), drops the cache and falls back to a full render.

Both the root message (`ContentWithMarkdown`) and streaming subagents (`AgentMessage`) now use it.

## Measured (same machine, `bun`)

Root message stream:

| Stream | Flushes | Total render CPU | Per flush | Worst flush |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 200 KB | 512 | 138 s → **0.62 s** (223×) | 270 ms → 1.2 ms | 14 s → **3.8 ms** |
| 50 KB | 128 | 6.4 s → **0.14 s** (44×) | 50 ms → 1.1 ms | 109 ms → 3.0 ms |
| 10 KB | 25 | 289 ms → **30 ms** (10×) | 11.6 ms → 1.2 ms | 19 ms → 2.0 ms |

Eight subagents streaming at once, 50 KB each:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Render work per flush | 275 ms | **8 ms** |
| Worst flush | 576 ms | **11 ms** |
| Total over 85 flushes | 23.4 s | **0.68 s** (35×) |

## Verification

The new test renders **both paths through a real terminal** (`@opentui/core/testing`) and compares `captureCharFrame()` - the actual characters on screen - at **every line boundary** of a document containing headings, paragraphs with emphasis/links/inline code, bullets, an ordered list, a blockquote, a table and a fenced code block. Frames are byte-identical, including inside an unterminated fence and at paragraph→list boundaries.

It also asserts a marker string is present in the frame, so an empty or error frame cannot pass the comparison vacuously (this caught a bug in the first version of the test, where both sides were rendering an error boundary).

- `bun test` (full CLI suite): **4202 pass, 0 fail** across 279 files
- `bun run typecheck`: exit 0

## Notes

`renderMarkdownNodes` is exported from the renderer for this, and `createRenderState` gained a key prefix so segment node keys stay unique without wrapper elements. `renderMarkdown` itself is unchanged.

ai.title: CLI streams markdown incrementally to avoid re-parsing
ai.summary: The CLI now parses only the newest tail of a streaming message instead of the entire accumulated answer on every flush, using a new streaming markdown cache that keeps already-rendered blocks memoized. A new module in the CLI utility layer introduces createStreamingMarkdownCache and renderStreamingMarkdownCached, and both the root message component and the agent message component use it while content is still streaming. When streaming finishes, or when the content is replaced rather than extended, the cache drops and the renderer falls back to a full parse so the final output matches a single render. Committed segments are wrapped in memo so React stops re-walking the stable prefix on each flush, which the PR notes took the worst flush cost from 38 ms to 3.8 ms.
ai.evidence: New file cli/src/utils/streaming-markdown.ts exports createStreamingMarkdownCache and renderStreamingMarkdownCached, which reuse the parse of the stable prefix of streaming markdown; cli/src/components/blocks/content-with-markdown.tsx and cli/src/components/message-with-agents.tsx now call renderStreamingMarkdownCached during streaming instead of the full parse

This saves computing effort and prevents the screen from freezing while long answers are still streaming. It affects anyone using the CLI, web assistant, or desktop app to chat with the AI. You will notice that long responses appear more smoothly and the interface stays responsive without stuttering.

acceptedPr.title: perf(cli): render one smaller page of transcript messages
acceptedPr.author: Salhi-zh
acceptedPr.body:
## Why

A re-render in opentui lays out **every rendered node**, and the cost is linear in that count whether or not the node changed:

| case (1,500 spans) | median per frame |
|---|---|
| re-render + paint | 59.2 ms |
| `renderOnce` with nothing re-rendered | **0.1 ms** |

So the cost is not a per-frame paint charge — an untouched tree is nearly free. It is paid per *re-render*, which is why memoizing cannot rescue it: a page of 15 memoized messages measured 15.0 ms against 13.1 ms for the same page unmemoized at 1,800 nodes. `@opentui/core@0.3.4` has no culling, so the only lever is how many nodes a page holds.

A streamed chunk re-renders the whole page. At the real density (~770 nodes per message) one page measures:

| page | nodes | median per frame |
|---|---|---|
| 15 messages (today) | 11,550 | 266.5 ms |
| 6 messages | 4,620 | **104.4 ms** |

## What

`MESSAGE_BATCH_SIZE` 15 → 6, with the measurement recorded next to the constant so the next reader knows it is a frame-cost knob and not a layout preference. `LoadPreviousButton` already renders the hidden count and loads a page at a time (`handleLoadPreviousMessages` adds `MESSAGE_BATCH_SIZE`), so the rest of the history is one click away and each load stays cheap.

## Verification

- `bun run typecheck` → exit 0
- `bun test` over all non-integration files: **3958 pass, 20 fail** — the same 20 import errors `main` has in a partial checkout (`Failed to load CLI environment … Cannot find module '../../../packages/internal/src/env'`); `main` alone measures 3951 pass / 20 fail.
- Frame timings above are `bun bench` runs against `@opentui/core`'s test renderer, not the app harness; the ratio is what the change buys.

## Trade-off

Fewer messages visible before clicking "load previous". If 6 is too aggressive, the number is independent of the mechanism — say which page size you want and I will re-measure it.

ai.title: Reduce CLI transcript message batch size to 6
ai.summary: The constant `MESSAGE_BATCH_SIZE` in the CLI's chat message hook `use-chat-messages.ts` is reduced from 15 to 6 to lower per-frame render costs during streaming. The accompanying comment documents that OpenTUI layouts every rendered node linearly, so a 15-message page of roughly 11,500 nodes measured 60 ms per frame, whereas 6 messages are roughly a third of that cost. Users can still access older messages via `LoadPreviousButton`, which loads an additional `MESSAGE_BATCH_SIZE` page on click.
ai.evidence: The diff modifies the `MESSAGE_BATCH_SIZE` constant in `cli/src/hooks/use-chat-messages.ts`, changing its value from 15 to 6 and expanding the doc comment to explain that OpenTUI re-render costs are linear in node count, making the 15-message page (~11.5k nodes) too expensive for streaming.

This change affects anyone using the free or paid terminal version of the assistant. You will see the same content, but when you scroll up to read older messages, you will need to click a load-more button slightly more often to reveal them.

Simultaneously, `MESSAGE_BATCH_SIZE` in `cli/src/hooks/use-chat-messages.ts` increases from 6 to 15, restoring a larger pagination window that previously caused ~11.5k node layouts per frame. The think-tag parser in `cli/src/utils/block-operations.ts` also reverts to scanning the combined text of the last block and incoming delta rather than using the optimized seam-scanning logic.
